CODE OF PRACTICE FOR INTERIOR ILLUMINATION
PART II SCHEDULE FOR VALUES OF ILLUMINATION AND GLARE INDEX I

0. FOREWORD
0.1 This Indian Standard (Part II ) was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 15 July 1966, .after the draft finalized by the Illuminating Engineering and Lifts Sectional Committee had been approved by the Electrotechnical Division Council. 0.2 A series of standards on interior This this is the second in the series. values and limiting values of glare the principles of good lighting and with the calculation of coefficients of illumination is being drawn up and part covers schedule for illumination Part I of this standard covers index. aspects of design and Part III deals utilization based on BZ classification.

0.3 For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test, shall be rounded off in accordance with IS : 2-1960*. The number of significant places retained in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard. 1. SCOPE 1.1 This standard ( Part 11) covers the recommended ' tion and limiting values of glare index. 2. TERMINOLOGY 2.1 For the purpose of this standard, standard shall apply. 3. SCHEDULE TION AND the definitions given in Part I of this values of illumina-

OF RECOMMENDED VALUES OF ILLUMINALIMITING VALUES OF GLARE INDEX

3.1 This schedule ( Table 1 ) gives values of illumination and limiting values of glare index commensurate with the general standards of lighting described in this code and related to many occupations and buildings. The great variety of visual tasks makes it impossible to list them all and those given should be regarded as representing types of task.
*Rules for rounding off numerical values ( reoisezi).

3

IS : 3646 ( Part II) - 1966 3.X.1 The different locations and tasks are grouped the following four sections: a) Industrial buildings and processes; b) Offices, schools and public buildings; c) Surgeries and hospitals; and d) Hotels, restaurants, shops and homes. alphabetically within

values (see Table 1) 3.2 lilumination Values - The illumination They recommended are those to be maintained at all times on the task. represent good modern practice and should be regarded as giving the order of illumination commonly required rather than as having some absolute significance. They may be exceeded where standards of visual performance or amenitv higher than those set in the code are called for provided that other requirements of the code, such as freedom from visual discomfort, are satisfied. 3.2.1 The recommended values increase by steps each of which is fairly large because it is related to a corresponding step in visual difficulty as The series is: between one class of scheduled task and the next. 10,20,30, 50, 70, 100, 150, 200, 300, 450, 700, 1 000, 1500, 2 000, 3 000 3.2.2 Where work takes tion to the recommended location of the tasks is not mended value is that on a place throughout an interior, general illuminavalue is necessary; where the precise height and known or cannot be easily specified, the recomhorizontal plane O-9 m above Boor level.

_

3.2.3 Where the work is localized, the recommended value is that for the task only; it need not, and sometimes should not, be the level of illumination used throughout the interior. Some prccesses, such as industrial inspection process, call for lighting of specialized design, where the level of illumination is only one of several factors to be taken into account. 3.3 Determining Illomination for Acceptable Visual Performance The appropriate value of illumination for a task not listed in Table 1 or which cannot be derived from it by analogy may be determined by the nomogram method given in -4ppendix A. 3.4 Glare Index -The value of glare index for a particular lighting installation when computed by the method given in Part I of this standard should not exceed the limiting value recommended in this schedule (set Table 1 ) for the appropriate location, The recommended limiting values of the glare index form a series whose steps indicate noticeable changes in glare. The series is: 10, 13, 16, 19, 22, 25, 28 The recommended limiting values of glare index apply to the location and not to the task; little glare is normally experienced when attention is concentrated on the task. They represent the maximum degree of glare which is acceptable for the room or building in which the particular 4

Iii : 3646 ( P2rt II ) - 1966 occupation is carried on. Where different occupations are carried on in the same room, the installation should be designed to the lowest value of glare index recommended for the ~different occupations.

APPENDIX ( czfzzm? 3.3)
NOMOGRAM A-l. NOMOGRAM

A

METHOD

A-1.1 A straight edge placed across the nomogram through the appropriate values of size and reflection factor will show the required illumination value in lux on the right-hand scale. A-l.2 This computed value of illuminntion may have to be increased or decreased to take account of special occupational conditions which justify The recommendation that the illumisome higher or lower illumination. nation of all normal working areas should not be less than 150 iux should be observed and if the computed value for any task is lower than this value it should not be used. A art from this general proviso, a computed value may be increased by a P actor of 1.5 to take account of specral practical circumstances such as when:

'

-

4

the interior has no natural lighting; the consequences of oversights or misperceptions would be very serious (for example, in surgery or when working on costly materials or with dangerous substances or apparatus ); personnel involved are of average age exceeding 40 years;

bl

Cl the 4 the

time in which the necessary details should be seen is fixed and brief; and goggles or the like have to be worn. applies, the factor of l-5 should

e) protective

If more than one special circumstance in general be used only once.

A-l.3 On the other hand, the computed illumination may be decreased by dividing by I.5 when, for example, the demand for critical vision is infrequent and is for brief periods only. In working areas, the effect of any such reduction is subject to the minimum illumination requirement for such areas.
After these adjustments have been made, the resulting illumination value is that suitable for use in practice.
